diagnostic_evidence.quote: the order of convergence of the degree $2q+1$ method is $q+1$

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem claims the bound |1-ℓ²|^{(q+1)^T} with d=2q+1. The proof's last two inequalities instead use exponent (d+1)^T=(2q+2)^T and then say 'as required'. The [q/0] Padé (Newton–Schulz-type) map has order q+1, so the chain with (d+1)^T is false. For d=3 it would assert |1-f(x)| ≤ |1-x²|^{4^T}/(1+f), but for T=1 the left side is about 1.5(1-x)² near x=1 while the right side is O((1-x)^4). The proof as written therefore does not establish the stated bound.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace (d+1)^T by (q+1)^T in the proof and re-derive the cited Kenney–Laub bound with the Padé order q+1 for the [q/0] approximant.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of the stated rate is wrong as written, so the quadratic (d=3) and cubic (d=5) convergence conclusions are unsupported by the argument given. With the correct exponent the statement itself is consistent with the Padé order.
issues.title: Proof of the convergence theorem derives exponent (d+1)^T, not the stated (q+1)^T
issues.why_classification: The statement is consistent with the Padé order. The fix is a local correction of the exponent in the proof; the theorem and its consequences are unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the method will eventually converge for any $\ell \in (0, u]$

issues.failure_explanation: The text claims that Theorem 4.2's guarantee extends to polynomials built from a wrong ℓ, including an overestimate ℓ in (σ_min, u), and that the method converges for any ℓ in (0,u]. Theorem 4.1 and the convergence theorem are proved only when [ℓ,u] contains the spectrum. For ℓ>σ_min some singular values lie outside the design interval, and no argument is given that the sequence ℓ_t, u_t stays valid for them. No comparison with Newton–Schulz is proved either. The claim rests on an informal 'somewhere between' and a citation to a degree-3 result of another paper. The setup is also stated inconsistently (ℓ'≥σ_min≥ℓ versus ℓ∈(σ_min,u)).

failure_location.quote: we obtain a polynomial whose convergence speed is somewhere between that of the optimal polynomial and Newton-Schulz

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either prove a lemma that, for σ_min<ℓ, the composed polynomials keep singular values positive, monotone and bounded by a Newton–Schulz-type rate in σ_min. Or restrict the claim to ℓ ≤ σ_min and present the other cases as empirical observations.
issues.overall_effect: The robustness-to-bad-ℓ claims, which justify guessing ℓ in practice, are asserted rather than proved. The formal theorems for correctly specified ℓ are unaffected.
issues.title: Unproved claim that the convergence guarantee extends to a mis-specified lower bound ℓ
issues.why_classification: A contained new argument or a narrowing of the claim suffices. The main theorems survive, but the robustness guarantee is lost unless it is proved.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: These adjustments stabilize the algorithm with a negligible effect on accuracy.

issues.failure_explanation: The relations ℓ_{t+1}=p_t(ℓ_t) and u_{t+1}=2-ℓ_{t+1} come from the minimax lemma. They hold for the exact minimiser on the design interval, and p(ℓ_design) is then the minimum there. In Algorithm 1, p_t is instead the minimiser on [max(ℓ_t,u_t/10),u_t] and is then composed with x→x/1.01. The cushion shifts the design endpoint away from ℓ_t, and the 1.01 scaling breaks the symmetry about 1. So [ℓ_{t+1},u_{t+1}] is not the true image and the polynomials are not the minimax ones. Theorem 4.1's optimality and the bound 1-ℓ_{T+1} are not established for the algorithm as stated. The proof of the convergence theorem nevertheless asserts that the algorithm returns p*(M). The pseudocode also omits the recentering step used in the code that generated the published coefficients. The 'negligible effect on accuracy' claim is unproved.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the guarantee only for the unmodified polynomials. For the stabilized version, compute the true image interval of each modified p_t (as the code does with recentering) and state the resulting bound, or present the optimality claim as approximate. Align the pseudocode with the code.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised worst-case optimality and the a-priori error bound hold for the idealized polynomials but are not proved for the instantiated, stabilized method. The pseudocode and code are not the same procedure.
issues.title: Stabilized Algorithm 1 no longer satisfies the interval recursion or optimal-polynomial guarantees it relies on
issues.why_classification: The ideal-case results survive. The repair is a contained reformulation (correct interval bookkeeping and a weaker, honest guarantee for the practical variant), not new global machinery.

issues.failure_explanation: The derivation needs max|1-p(x)| ≤ (1-ℓ/u)³ for the degree-5 Padé polynomial p. In fact, with y=x/u, 1-p(y)=(1-y)³(8+9y+3y²)/8, which is about 2.5(1-y)³ near y=1. For example, at y=0.9 the error is 0.00232 > 0.001=(0.1)³. A bound of the form |1-x²|³ would give a constant 8, not 1. So the displayed inequality is false, and the conclusion |p*-p| ≤ 2ε_double at the threshold should read about 5ε_double.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the bound by max|1-p| ≤ 2.5(1-ℓ/u)³ (from the exact factorization) and adjust the constants, or tighten the threshold by a constant factor.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed 'equal to p up to double precision machine epsilon' accuracy at the shortcut threshold is off by a small constant factor. The shortcut is still essentially valid.
issues.title: Early-return justification in the degree-5 Remez algorithm uses a false constant in the Padé error bound
issues.why_classification: A one-line constant correction with no change to the method, threshold order, or conclusions.
